Family Health

Painful ejaculation: possible causes, assessment and care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pain during or after ejaculation can range from mild discomfort to severe pain in the penis, scrotum or perineum, the area between the scrotum and anus. Terms such as dysorgasmia or orgasmalgia describe pain linked to orgasm, which can also happen without semen being released. Pain can affect confidence, intimacy and daily life. It deserves assessment without embarrassment or an assumption about the cause.

When to arrange care and when it is urgent

Contact a clinician for new, repeated or persistent pain with ejaculation or orgasm, particularly with burning urine, discharge, blood in urine or semen, a changed urine stream or a new lump. Primary care or a sexual-health service can begin the assessment and arrange urology referral when needed. Tell a cancer-treatment or surgical team about symptoms after their treatment. Get urgent same-day advice for visible or suspected blood in urine, even once, in a small amount or if you are unsure it is blood.

Seek urgent same-day advice for fever or shaking chills with urinary or pelvic pain, rapidly worsening symptoms or feeling very unwell. Inability to pass urine, sudden severe testicular pain, severe lower-abdominal pain, confusion or serious breathing difficulty needs emergency care. Do not wait for a routine sexual-health appointment if these occur.

Prostatitis and infection are not the same in every case

The prostate contributes fluid to semen. Prostatitis describes inflammation involving the prostate and sometimes nearby tissues. Bacterial infection is one cause; chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome can occur without an identified bacterial infection. Painful ejaculation, urinary burning or frequency, lower-abdominal discomfort and erection difficulties can overlap, so symptoms alone do not establish the type.

Previous urinary infection, urinary procedures or a catheter, enlarged-prostate obstruction, diabetes, reduced immunity and sexual exposures can be relevant to the history. They are not a checklist that proves prostatitis or blame for an infection. Acute bacterial illness may need prompt antibiotics or hospital care; chronic pelvic pain often requires a different approach.

Surgery, radiotherapy and changes in orgasm

Prostate surgery or hernia repair can be associated with pain during sexual activity, sometimes through scarring, nerve effects or other postoperative problems. Radical prostatectomy removes the whole prostate and seminal vesicles, rather than only part of the gland. Ejaculation of semen normally stops afterwards, but orgasm can still occur and can sometimes be painful. Report painful dry orgasms as well as pain when semen is released.

Pelvic radiotherapy can affect sexual function and cause discomfort. Some effects improve during recovery; others develop later or persist. Do not assume all radiation effects are temporary or that new pain is an unavoidable effect to tolerate. The treating team can assess infection, scarring or other problems and discuss appropriate rehabilitation.

Cysts, stones and blockage of the ejaculatory ducts

An obstruction in the ducts carrying semen, sometimes related to a cyst or stone, is one possible cause of pain or blood in semen. It can also affect fertility, but pain does not by itself mean obstruction or infertility. Low semen volume, fertility concerns and previous procedures may help determine whether specialist tests are appropriate.

A urologist may consider targeted imaging and semen testing when the history warrants it. A procedure to open an obstructed duct or a fertility treatment is an option in selected cases, not a mandatory operation for every cyst or painful ejaculation. Discuss the evidence, risks, alternatives and whether treatment is intended to address pain, fertility or both.

Medicines, including antidepressants

Antidepressants can affect desire, erection, ejaculation or orgasm; painful ejaculation has also been reported. SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic or tetracyclic medicines and monoamine oxidase inhibitors have different side-effect profiles. A symptom beginning after a medicine or dose change is useful information, but does not prove that the drug is responsible.

Do not suddenly stop an antidepressant or change its dose yourself. Withdrawal and relapse can cause harm. Tell the prescriber about timing, other medicines and the effect on sexual life. They may review the diagnosis, adjust treatment or discuss alternatives, balancing mental-health benefit and side effects; finding a suitable plan may take time.

Pudendal nerve and pelvic-floor pain

The pudendal nerve supplies areas of the pelvis and genitals. Irritation or injury may cause burning, shooting pain, tingling or numbness, sometimes worse with sitting or sexual activity. Pelvic injury, surgery, diabetes or neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis may be relevant, but they do not prove a pudendal diagnosis; other causes need consideration.

A pelvic-health physiotherapist may assess muscle tenderness and coordination and use an individual plan, including relaxation when muscles are overactive. Repeated strengthening or Kegel exercises are not suitable for every painful pelvic floor. Specialist options can include nerve-pain medicines, selected injections or nerve blocks, and occasionally surgery for confirmed compression after other care fails. None guarantees relief.

Sexually transmitted infections and partner care

Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection that can cause genital or urinary irritation and may be associated with ejaculation discomfort. Other infections can cause urethritis or prostatitis too. Symptoms may be absent, and pain cannot identify the organism. Give an honest exposure history and ask which tests, including other STI tests, are appropriate.

Confirmed trichomoniasis needs an effective prescribed oral antimicrobial; not every antibiotic works, and a topical product is not a substitute. Current partners need concurrent treatment to prevent reinfection. Avoid sex until both you and partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. Follow the service’s advice about follow-up and retesting; do not share leftover medicines.

Cancer concerns without assuming a cancer diagnosis

Prostate cancer often has no symptoms early on. Urinary changes, erection difficulties or blood in urine or semen can have many causes, and painful ejaculation alone does not diagnose cancer. Tell the clinician about persistent symptoms, age, family history and previous cancer treatment so they can decide which investigation is useful.

If cancer is diagnosed, treatment depends on its risk, stage, spread, general health and personal priorities. Options can include surgery, radiotherapy, hormone therapy and selected chemotherapy, targeted or immune treatments. For suitable low-risk disease, active surveillance involves planned tests and follow-up, not minimal attention. No single cancer treatment is prescribed just because ejaculation hurts.

Stress, relationships and a respectful assessment

Stress, anxiety and relationship difficulties can influence pain, muscle tension and sexual experience. Pain occurring with a partner but not during masturbation is useful context, but it does not prove a psychological cause or exclude a physical problem. Sometimes no single cause is found despite appropriate assessment.

Psychosexual counselling or psychological support may help with distress and coping alongside medical or pelvic-pain care. It should not replace examination of concerning symptoms or imply that the pain is imagined. You can ask for an explanation of a proposed examination, consent to it and request appropriate support or a chaperone.

What the appointment and tests may involve

Prepare to describe when pain began, whether it happens during or after orgasm, how long it lasts and whether semen is released. Note other genital or urinary symptoms, medicines and dose changes, surgery or radiotherapy, sexual exposures, diabetes, neurological illness and family history. A focused examination may include the abdomen and genitals and, when appropriate, a rectal examination of the prostate.

Urine testing or culture, STI tests and selected blood, semen or imaging tests may be useful. PSA testing requires an individual discussion: prostate inflammation can raise it, and a result alone does not diagnose cancer. Not everyone needs a PSA test, rectal examination or scan. Persistent symptoms after treatment deserve reassessment rather than repeating the same treatment indefinitely.

Treatment, comfort and talking with a partner

Care follows the cause. Bacterial prostatitis may need a clinician-selected antibiotic course; severe infection may require intravenous treatment. Anti-inflammatory pain relief is suitable only for some people. Postoperative pain, obstruction, nerve pain and chronic pelvic pain need different plans, and underlying diabetes or neurological disease should also be managed. Do not self-prescribe antibiotics, steroid injections or a procedure.

Avoid pushing through painful sexual activity. Choose a calm, unhurried time to explain what hurts, how it affects you and what assessment you are arranging; listen to your partner’s concerns without treating pain as rejection. Agree on comfortable forms of intimacy without pressure. Record symptoms and review progress with the clinician. Many causes can be treated or managed, but timing and outcome vary and improvement cannot be guaranteed.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

EAU guidance lists several associations with painful ejaculation and supports cause-based care while noting limited evidence for surgery for pain alone.

AUA 2025 guidance supports individualized pelvic-floor therapy, including relaxation for increased muscle tone, and medical assessment before dismissing symptoms as psychological.

NCI and Prostate Cancer UK clarify radical prostatectomy, dry orgasm and structured cancer surveillance; treatment effects may be persistent.

CDC guidance supports specific trichomoniasis treatment, concurrent partner treatment and avoiding sex until treatment completion and symptom resolution.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to note symptom timing, urine or semen changes, medicines, treatments and questions. These notes can support an appointment; they cannot diagnose infection, nerve injury or cancer, assess fertility or choose a treatment.

When to seek help

Seek prompt advice for fever, chills, urinary pain, blood, discharge or worsening symptoms. Inability to urinate, sudden severe testicular pain, severe abdominal pain, confusion or serious breathing difficulty needs emergency care. Do not stop prescribed medicines, force painful activity or attempt procedures yourself. This is general education, not individual diagnosis.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pain with ejaculation or orgasm is a symptom with several possible causes, including painful dry orgasm after prostate surgery.
  • Fever with pelvic or urinary pain needs prompt advice; inability to urinate or sudden severe testicular pain needs emergency care.
  • Antibiotics, surgery and pelvic-floor exercises are not universal treatments.
  • Do not stop antidepressants or other necessary medicines without prescriber advice.
  • Assessment and open, pressure-free communication can support care; symptoms do not prove cancer or a psychological cause.

Frequently asked questions

What problems can painful ejaculation cause?

Pain can affect sexual confidence, relationships and quality of life. Some underlying conditions need treatment, but pain does not automatically mean a dangerous illness or infertility. Assessment helps identify the next step.

Can surgery cause pain even without semen?

Yes. After radical prostatectomy the whole prostate and seminal vesicles are removed, so semen is no longer ejaculated. Orgasm can still happen and can be painful; tell the surgical team about a painful dry orgasm.

Does it mean prostate cancer?

No. Prostate cancer is one possible context, but infection, pelvic pain, treatment effects and other causes are possible. Persistent symptoms or blood need review; a symptom or PSA result alone does not diagnose cancer.

When should I contact a clinician?

Arrange assessment for new, recurring or persistent pain, especially with urinary changes, discharge or blood. Fever with urinary or pelvic pain requires prompt same-day advice. Inability to urinate, sudden severe testicular pain or severe systemic illness needs emergency care.

Should I stop my antidepressant?

No, not on your own. Report the pain and its timing to the prescriber. They can assess possible causes and discuss a gradual, supervised change if appropriate; abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal or relapse.

Should I strengthen my pelvic floor?

Not automatically. Painful muscles may be overactive and need relaxation or coordination work rather than repeated tightening. A trained pelvic-health therapist can assess which approach suits you.

Does pain only with a partner prove it is emotional?

No. Differences between situations are helpful history, but do not establish a psychological cause. Medical assessment and appropriate psychological or relationship support can be combined.

How are partners managed for trichomoniasis?

Current partners need concurrent treatment. Avoid sex until all have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved, and follow local advice about other STI testing and follow-up. Pain alone cannot diagnose trichomoniasis.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
